scenario: You are stranded with water and shelter but no known food, and you decide to use the Universal Edibility Test (UET) on the leaves of a plentiful plant that is not in the carrot family and has no milky sap. You have fasted for 8 hours and separated the leaves from the rest of the plant. What do you do FIRST with the leaf?

options.text: Boil a small piece for 15 minutes and taste it - cooking destroys most toxins
Crush a piece and hold it against your inner wrist for 15 minutes, watching for a reaction
Eat a thumbnail-sized piece and wait 8 hours before eating more
Crush it and smell it - reject it if it has a strong bitter, acidic, or almond smell

explanation: The smell check comes first because it costs nothing and rules out some dangerous plants before you touch them. The order is: smell, skin contact (about 15 minutes, then watch for hours), lips, tongue (15 minutes), chew (15 minutes), swallow a small bite and wait 8 hours, then eat about 1/4 cup and wait another 8 hours. Any reaction means stop. Skin contact (b) is the second step, not the first. Eating a piece right away (c) skips every safety gate. Boiling (a) does not destroy many plant toxins. Remember the test's real limits: it cannot reliably catch deadly plants like water hemlock, and it never works for mushrooms - use it only as a last resort.

scenario: You have 4 pounds of fresh venison. The power has been out for 5 days and will not return soon. It is 65°F outside. Which plan keeps this meat safe the longest without refrigeration?

options.text: Hang it in a cool, shaded spot - air circulation will slow spoilage
Slice it thin, heat the strips to 160°F, then dry them at 140°F or higher until they crack when bent
Lay strips in the sun on rocks for a day - sunlight kills bacteria
Seal it in jars and simmer them in a pot of boiling water (water-bath canning)

explanation: Making jerky with a heat step is the safest choice. Trim the fat, slice 1/4 inch thick, heat the strips to 160°F (71°C) to kill bacteria like E. coli, then dry at a steady 140°F until a strip bends and cracks but does not snap. Stored airtight in a cool, dark place, homemade jerky keeps about 1 to 3 weeks. Hanging raw meat at 65°F (a) spoils it within a day or two. Sun drying (c) at mild temperatures is too slow and does not heat meat enough to kill germs. Water-bath canning (d) is unsafe for meat - low-acid foods need a pressure canner to prevent botulism.

scenario: Your group is short on calories and must choose where to spend foraging effort. Rank these foods from HIGHEST to LOWEST calories per 100 grams of edible portion.

items.text: Lean freshwater fish such as sunfish (raw weight)

explanation: Nuts are the most calorie-dense wild plant foods because of their fat: pine nuts have roughly 670 calories per 100 g. Dried acorn meal is also high, around 400 to 500 calories per 100 g, but only after the tannins are leached out. Lean fish is a great protein source but has under 100 calories per 100 g raw, and eating only lean meat for days can make you sick without fat or carbohydrates. Dandelion greens have about 45 calories per 100 g - good for vitamins, but nearly useless for energy. Lesson: when calories are short, put effort into fats and starches first, then protein, and treat greens as a vitamin supplement.

scenario: Along a roadside ditch you find a tall plant with white, umbrella-shaped flower clusters, fern-like leaves, and a smooth, hairless stem with purple blotches. Crushed leaves smell musty. A friend says it is wild carrot and the root is edible. What should you do?

options.text: Dig up the root and boil it well - cooking removes the toxins
Do not eat it - these features match poison hemlock, which can kill
Do the universal edibility test on the root to be sure
Eat only the leaves, since the toxins are in the root

explanation: A smooth stem with purple blotches and a musty, mousy smell are classic signs of poison hemlock. Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) has a hairy stem without purple blotches. All parts of poison hemlock are toxic, including leaves (d), and cooking or drying does not make it safe (a). The edibility test (c) is not reliable for deadly carrot-family plants - even a small taste can be fatal. With white umbrella-shaped flowers, the safe answer is to leave the plant alone, wear gloves if you touch it, and never burn it.

scenario: A neighbor cooked white wild mushrooms from a park on Saturday night. On Sunday morning he had vomiting and watery diarrhea. By Monday he feels much better and says he will skip the doctor. What is the right advice?

options.text: He is fine - feeling better means the mushroom has passed through
Drink lots of fluids and only see a doctor if he gets sick again
Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) and get to a hospital now - this pattern fits death cap poisoning
Take activated charcoal at home; the mushroom was cooked, so the toxin is weakened

explanation: Amatoxin mushrooms like death caps and destroying angels cause stomach symptoms 6 to 24 hours after eating, then a 'false recovery,' then severe liver damage 2 to 4 days later. Feeling better (a, b) is exactly the dangerous phase. Cooking, boiling, freezing, and drying do not destroy amatoxins (d). Call Poison Control right away and get hospital care - early treatment can save the liver. Bring any leftover mushrooms and photos. California's 2025-2026 outbreak caused dozens of poisonings, several deaths, and liver transplants.

scenario: An ice storm knocked out power three days ago and it is raining hard. You want to cook dinner on your propane camp stove. Where is it safe to use it?

options.text: In the attached garage with the big door open
In the kitchen next to an open window
Outside, away from doors, windows, and vents, under an open shelter such as a canopy
In the kitchen, as long as you only run it for 10 minutes

explanation: Camp stoves, grills, and generators make carbon monoxide, which you cannot see or smell. CDC guidance is to never use them inside a home, garage, or carport, or near doors, windows, or vents. An open garage door (a) or window (b) does not clear CO reliably, and even short use indoors (d) can poison people. Cook outside under an open canopy set well away from the house, and run battery-powered CO alarms indoors. Headache, dizziness, or nausea in several people means get outside and call 911.

scenario: You are cleaning a rabbit taken during a legal season. You have a small cut on one finger. When you open the body, the liver is covered with many small white spots. What do you do?

options.text: Cut away the liver and cook the rest of the meat well
Discard the whole carcass, disinfect your tools, wash well, and watch for fever or a skin sore over the next two weeks
Rinse the meat in salt water and cook it to 145°F
Keep going - white spots are normal fat deposits in wild rabbits

explanation: Many white or yellow spots on a rabbit's liver or spleen can be a sign of tularemia or another disease. Do not eat any of it (a, c, d). Bag and dispose of the carcass following local rules, clean tools with bleach solution, and wash your hands well. Tularemia can enter through small cuts, which is why CDC advises wearing gloves when handling rabbits and rodents. Watch for sudden fever, chills, swollen glands, or a sore at the cut, usually 3 to 5 days later, and see a doctor if they appear. Also note 145°F is too low for game - cook it to at least 160°F, ideally 165°F.

scenario: You caught several perch from a lake during a long power outage. Someone wants to make 'lake ceviche' by soaking raw fillets in lime juice for an hour. What is the safest way to eat these fish?

options.text: Ceviche is fine - the acid in lime juice cooks the fish
Freeze them in the chest freezer that lost power, then eat them raw
Cook them until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily, or 145°F inside
Smoke them lightly for 20 minutes - smoke kills parasites

explanation: Wild freshwater fish can carry parasites such as fish tapeworm. Acid marinades (a) and light smoking (d) do not reliably kill parasites. Freezing only works at very low temperatures - such as -4°F for 7 days - which a home freezer, let alone one without power (b), may not reach. Cook fish to 145°F (63°C) or until opaque and flaky all the way through. Also check your state's fish advisory, since cooking does not remove mercury or PCBs.

scenario: Your household of five (two adults, a pregnant teenager, a 6-year-old, and a grandparent with diabetes) has about 3 weeks of shelf-stable food and no idea when stores will reopen. Fridge food is already used up. How should you ration?

options.text: Cut everyone to half rations equally - fairness matters most
Healthy adults cut back and rest more; keep full rations for the child and the pregnant teen, and follow the grandparent's diabetes meal plan
Eat normally until food runs out, then figure it out
Cut food and water by half for everyone to stretch both supplies

explanation: Emergency guidance says healthy adults who reduce activity can live on about half their usual food for an extended time, but children and pregnant women should not be rationed. People with diabetes need steady meals that match their medicine, so follow their care plan. Equal cuts (a) put the most vulnerable at risk. Eating normally (c) wastes the chance to stretch supplies. Never ration water (d) - dehydration is far more dangerous than hunger.

scenario: You are packing a long-term food supply in Mylar bags with oxygen absorbers. Which item should NOT be sealed in an oxygen-free bag at room temperature, and why?

options.text: White rice - it will absorb the oxygen absorber's iron
Dry pinto beans - they need oxygen to stay edible
Home-dried fruit that is still soft and moist - moist food without oxygen can grow botulism
Wheat berries - they will sprout in the bag

explanation: Oxygen absorbers are meant for dry foods, about 10 percent moisture or less, such as white rice, dry beans, and wheat. Sealing moist foods without oxygen creates conditions where botulism bacteria can grow, as Utah State University Extension warns. Rice (a), beans (b), and wheat (d) store well this way when dry. Keep sealed containers cool (ideally 40 to 60°F), dark, and off the floor, since every rise of about 10°F roughly halves storage life.

start.scenario: Day 4 of a true life-or-death emergency with no resupply in sight. You are in a temperate woodland with one partner and have not eaten in 48 hours. You have 3 meters of 550 paracord, a knife, and a pair of nitrile gloves. You've found active rabbit runs - fresh tracks and droppings on 3 separate trails. (Outside an emergency like this, snaring is illegal or regulated in most states.) What is your trapping strategy?

options.text: Set multiple small snares on the rabbit runs using the paracord
Construct a deadfall trap (Paiute or figure-4) at the most active trail

multiple_snares.scenario: Good. You pull the inner strands out of the paracord to make several thin snare loops. How do you set them?

options.text: Set 3 snares - one on each active run - and check them every few hours
Set 2 snares and keep 1 m of paracord in reserve for other uses

three_snares.explanation: More good sets on active trails means more chances for a meal. Hang each loop about 3 to 4 inches across, roughly a fist's height above the trail, anchored to a stake or root, and disturb the trail as little as possible. Check at least daily, and more often in warm weather, because caught animals spoil and attract predators. Put on gloves before handling a catch - rabbits can carry tularemia - and do not eat one that looks sick or has many white spots on its liver. Cook rabbit to at least 160-165°F, and eat some fat or starch with it, since rabbit is very lean. Take down every snare when you leave.

two_snares_reserve.explanation: Two snares can work but cut your odds. You catch nothing on the first check, move one snare to a fresher trail, and get a rabbit a day later. Keeping cord in reserve is reasonable planning, but trapping success rises with the number of good sets - and you can recover the cord from the snares later. Whatever you catch, wear gloves to handle it, check it for signs of illness, and cook it thoroughly.

single_deadfall.explanation: A deadfall needs precise trigger pieces and careful tuning. You spend 2+ hours building it, burning energy you cannot spare, and the rabbit avoids the unfamiliar object. No catch in 24 hours. Deadfalls can also injure your hands while setting. With 3 active runs and cord on hand, several simple snares will usually beat a single deadfall for most people. Match the method to your skill and materials.
